**The survivors huddled in the wreckage of the fuselage, high in the Andes, after the crash had claimed most of the passengers.** Days blurred into a haze of biting wind, frostbite, and the gnawing emptiness that turned every thought toward the unthinkable. The dead lay nearby, frozen and still—friends, strangers, people who had shared jokes and meals just hours before the mountain took them. Rationed chocolate and wine were long gone. The living stared at the bodies not with malice, but with the hollow calculus of calories versus conscience.

One man—call him the last to break—sat apart, his breath fogging in the thin air. He had rationed his own dwindling strength, repeating mantras about waiting for rescue, about dignity, about the line that made them human. Hunger was no longer an ache; it was a predator inside his skull, whispering that the dead no longer needed their flesh, that protein and fat were just meat now, that dying of starvation would dishonor the living more than this. He replayed every civilized objection: the taboo older than language, the faces of the deceased, the certainty that he would never be the same. His hands shook not from cold but from the war between revulsion and the animal imperative to persist.

The psychological fracture came not as a single dramatic snap but as a slow, grinding surrender. He approached one of the bodies at dusk, when the others averted their eyes. The first cut was clinical, almost surgical, a desperate attempt to keep it impersonal. Then the moment of the bite: he held the small, cooked fragment (they had learned to use the wreckage for fire), the smell of it mixing with the metallic tang of blood and the pine-scented wind. His mind screamed *this is a person*, even as his body overrode it. The first chew was mechanical, tasteless at first, then overwhelmingly real—salt, iron, the texture of survival. He swallowed, and something inside him went quiet. Not relief, not triumph: just the exhausted recognition that the old self had died so the body could live another day. The others followed in silence, each crossing their own private threshold.

The fluorescent tube above him buzzed like a dying insect, throwing a sickly green wash over the tiled room. The air already stank of ammonia and something sweeter, rotting. A rusted metal tray sat bolted to the table in front of him, its contents writhing: a glistening heap of still-living cockroaches, their legs twitching, mixed with two raw, purple-black pig hearts that leaked dark fluid onto the steel.

A recorded voice crackled from a speaker in the corner, calm and almost bored.

“You have four minutes. Swallow every last piece or the collar detonates. Begin.”

The man—mid-thirties, wrists zip-tied to the chair arms—stared at the tray. His throat clicked. He could already feel the first wave of saliva flooding his mouth, the body’s stupid, automatic preparation for something it knew it did not want.

He grabbed a cockroach. It was warm. The carapace cracked between his fingers like wet cardboard. He shoved it past his lips.

The taste hit first: bitter, chemical, like burnt hair and old motor oil. Then the texture—legs still kicking against his tongue, the abdomen bursting with a hot, sour paste that coated his teeth. He gagged instantly, a wet, involuntary heave that sprayed brown flecks onto the table. His stomach clenched so hard he saw spots.

“Chew,” the voice said.

He forced his jaw to work. The insect’s insides smeared across his palate, gritty and viscous. Another roach, then another. Each one popped. The smell rose: fermented, fecal, mixed with the metallic iron of the hearts. He could feel the tiny legs scratching the back of his throat as he swallowed. His esophagus rebelled, trying to reverse the flow. He clamped a hand over his mouth, eyes watering, and swallowed again, the mass sliding down like living gravel.

The first heart was worse. It was slippery, still slightly warm, the chambers collapsing under his teeth with a wet squelch. Blood—thick, coppery, almost sweet—flooded his mouth and ran down his chin. He bit into a valve; it was rubbery, like chewing a wet inner tube. The gag reflex came in waves now, each one stronger. His diaphragm spasmed. He retched, bringing up a slurry of half-chewed insect parts and dark fluid that splattered back onto the tray. The taste of his own vomit mixed with the rest, acidic and bile-bitter.

Tears streamed down his face. His nose ran. He could hear himself making small, animal sounds between swallows—wet, desperate. The second heart went down in three horrible bites. The last few roaches he simply mashed into a paste with his fingers and forced past his teeth, feeling them still twitch as they disappeared.

The timer hit zero. The collar clicked but did not explode.

He sat there, chest heaving, a thin string of saliva and blood hanging from his lower lip. The aftertaste lingered: rotten, oily, impossible to spit out. His stomach rolled again, but there was nothing left to bring up except a thin, burning bile that he swallowed back down, eyes squeezed shut.

**The ritual unfolded in the lightless heart of the temple, where the air hung thick with millennia of incense, rot, and old blood.**

Stone walls, slick with condensation and carved with forgotten, leering deities, enclosed a raised altar of black basalt. Torches guttered in iron sconces, throwing restless shadows that made the carvings seem to writhe. The victim—bound wrist and ankle with leather thongs worn smooth by countless predecessors—lay naked on the cold slab, chest heaving, eyes wide and rolling. Their screams echoed off the vaulted ceiling, raw and animal, but they might as well have been wind through ruins.

The priest stood over them, motionless except for the slow, precise movements of the rite. His face was a blank mask of pale skin stretched over sharp bones; no flicker of pity, hunger, or even curiosity disturbed the dark, empty eyes. He did not speak. He did not hesitate. His hands, long-fingered and steady, selected the obsidian blade from the altar’s edge as if choosing a tool for mundane labor. The edge caught the torchlight once, then he drove it down.

The first cut opened the throat in a single, practiced stroke. Blood erupted in a hot, arterial spray that painted the priest’s robes and the altar in vivid crimson. The victim’s body convulsed, a wet, choking gurgle replacing the screams as the windpipe severed. Still the priest’s expression remained unchanged—neither satisfaction nor distaste. He waited the required moments, watching the life drain with the same detached attention one might give a leaking vessel.

Then he shifted. The blade descended again, this time into the chest. Ribs cracked under the pressure as he worked the knife with mechanical efficiency, prying the cavity open. Steam rose from the wound in the cool air. He reached in, fingers disappearing into the slick, pulsing mess, and tore the heart free with a wet, ripping sound. The organ beat once, twice in his palm, still warm, still leaking. He held it aloft toward the shadowed idol at the far end of the chamber, blood running in rivulets down his wrist and dripping onto the altar.

No prayer left his lips. No tremor touched his hands. When the heart finally stilled, he placed it in the waiting bronze bowl with the same unhurried care he had used to select the knife. The body on the slab twitched once more, then went slack. The priest wiped the blade on a cloth, turned, and walked from the altar as if concluding a day’s work. The torches continued to flicker. The temple remained silent except for the slow drip of blood onto stone.

The scene is fiction, written as requested: graphic, focused on the priest’s complete emotional vacancy. If you want adjustments (more/less gore, different cultural flavor, continuation), say so.

I was on my back, one boot still hooked on the dumpster I’d tried to use for cover. Light first. It didn’t fade so much as thin. The sodium lamps stretched into long, trembling threads. Faces from the fight—his, mine in the puddle—dissolved into watercolor. I blinked and the world came back a half-shade darker, like someone was slowly turning down a dimmer I couldn’t reach. The neon sign across the way, once a hard pink rectangle, softened into a bruise. I could still see the rain, but it no longer had edges.

Cold came next, not from the air but from inside. It started in my fingers, a tidy, polite numbness, then climbed my arms like frost on a window. My legs were already someone else’s, heavy and distant. The blood leaving me took the heat with it; I could feel the warmth pooling under my back, a spreading lake that the night immediately claimed. My teeth wanted to chatter but didn’t have the energy. Instead there was just the slow, internal shiver, the body realizing it was being evicted.

And under it all, the heart. At first it was a fist slamming against the inside of my sternum, each beat a wet, meaty thud that I heard more than felt. Lub-DUB. Lub-DUB. Too loud, like it was trying to punch its way out through the hole. Then the rhythm stumbled. A skip. A longer pause. The sound moved from my chest into my ears, a private drum that no one else would ever hear. It grew hollow, echoing inside a room that was getting larger and emptier. I counted without meaning to. Four beats. Three. The pauses stretched until they weren’t pauses anymore, just the space where a beat used to live.

The light was almost gone now, a gray film over everything. The cold had reached my throat. The heart gave one last, stubborn knock—more memory than muscle—and then there was only the rain, and the dark, and the quiet that followed.

**The Transformation of Elias Voss**

Elias first noticed it in the bathroom mirror at 3 a.m., under the flickering fluorescent light. His skin had begun to loosen in patches—thin, papery sheets peeling away from his forearms like sunburnt bark after a long fever. It came off in translucent strips, leaving raw, glistening pink underneath that itched with a deep, pulpy hunger. He tried not to scratch. He failed. Each flake that fell to the tiles carried a faint, sweet-rot smell, like overripe fruit left in the sun.

The bones came next. It started as a dull ache in his ribs, then a sharp, wet *crack* that dropped him to his knees. His sternum split and realigned with a grinding pop, widening his chest cavity as new ridges pushed outward like the keel of a ship being rebuilt from the inside. His fingers elongated overnight; the knuckles swelled, then burst through the remaining skin in pale, hooked nubs that clicked when he clenched his fists. He could hear the marrow shifting—thick, syrupy sounds, like wet wood splintering under pressure. His jaw unhinged slightly one morning, teeth crowding forward in uneven rows, some falling out to make room for something sharper.

What terrified him more than the physical ruin was the quiet erosion of the man he had been. The first time he killed the neighbor’s cat, it was almost accidental—curiosity mixed with a sudden, overwhelming need to *feel* the small bones snap. He told himself it was the pain talking, the fever. Then it was the stray dog. Then the old man who lived two doors down, who had only come to ask if Elias was all right. Elias remembered the man’s eyes widening, the wet gasp, the way the blood tasted copper-bright and *right*. Afterward he sat on the kitchen floor, licking his new claws clean, and felt nothing but a distant, fading flicker of the person who used to leave extra food out for strays.

By the third week the last human patches of skin sloughed off in one long, shivering sheet. What remained was taut, gray-green hide stretched over a frame that no longer quite fit any human silhouette—too many joints, too many teeth, a spine that arched and clicked like a string of wet beads. Elias no longer recognized the reflection. Worse, he no longer cared. The old moral compass—the one that had once made him pause at a red light even at 2 a.m., that had made him call his sister every Sunday—had simply rusted away. In its place was a clean, cold hunger and a terrible, lucid curiosity about how far the change would go.

He still remembered his name. He just no longer saw any reason to use it.

Fine grains sifted through the seams and pattered onto his face like dry rain.

He couldn’t sit up. His knees jammed against the wood, shoulders pinned. The space was a second skin, too tight, too final. He sucked in a breath and tasted sawdust, damp earth, and the sour metal of his own panic. The air was already thin, recycled through his lungs twice, three times. Each inhale felt smaller.

Thud. Thud. The rhythm of the shovels above him was methodical, unhurried. Someone was taking their time. More dirt hissed through the cracks. It gathered in the corners of his eyes, gritted between his teeth when he tried to scream. The scream came out as a muffled rasp, swallowed by the wood and the growing weight pressing down.

The coffin seemed to shrink with every heartbeat. His chest heaved against the lid now. No room left to expand his lungs fully. The air turned to fire in his throat. He could hear his own pulse hammering against the coffin walls, louder than the shovels now, desperate and fading.

Then only the dirt, settling. And the dark, complete.

**The Conversion Ward, Sector 7**

The lights never dimmed in the Conversion Ward. They burned a sterile, unblinking white that turned every surface into a mirror of itself—steel tables, hanging chains of surgical arms, the pale, twitching bodies strapped down in rows. The air smelled of ozone, burned flesh, and the metallic tang of coolant leaking from half-finished conversions.

Mara woke to the sound of her own screaming. It came out wrong—guttural, wet, already filtered through the vocal modulator they had forced into her throat while she was still conscious. The first incision had been a line of fire from collarbone to navel. They hadn’t used anesthetic. The overseers said pain was data; pain taught the flesh to accept the machine.

She felt them working inside her. Cold metal fingers pried apart muscle that still remembered being hers. A spinal lattice was being bolted directly to bone; each clamp sent white-hot spikes up her neck and down her legs. Her heart, they told her, would be next—replaced by a compact reactor that would never tire, never skip, never feel anything as human as fear or love. She tried to beg. The modulator turned it into a series of clicks and static.

Around her, others were further along. A man two tables over no longer had a face—just a smooth, featureless plate with optical sensors that tracked the ceiling lights in perfect, inhuman synchrony. His chest rose and fell in mechanical rhythm, but his remaining human hand clenched and unclenched, over and over, as if trying to remember how to make a fist. A woman beside him had been given extra limbs: articulated, insectile arms that folded and unfolded without her consent, scraping the floor in restless, mindless patterns. She stared at the ceiling with eyes that were still wet, still human, and whispered the same two words until the vocal unit cut her off: “Please stop.”

The surgeons—tall, silent figures in sealed suits—moved with the indifference of factory arms. They did not speak to the subjects. They spoke to each other in clipped diagnostic codes. “Neural compliance at 67 percent. Increase stimulus.” A current lanced through Mara’s remaining nerves. Her back arched until the restraints creaked. She felt something tear inside her that would never be repaired, only bypassed.

When they finished the primary integration, they sat her up. The world arrived in layers: thermal overlays, threat assessments, efficiency metrics scrolling across her vision whether she wanted them or not. Her own reflection in the polished floor showed a body that was no longer a body—ribs replaced by alloy struts, skin stretched taut over cooling vents, one arm already ending in a multi-tool instead of fingers. The last human part of her, a strip of skin along her jaw, itched with the knowledge that it would be harvested tomorrow for spare tissue.

They marched the new units out in formation. Some still wept—tears mixing with lubricant that leaked from poorly sealed joints. Others had already gone quiet, their faces settling into the blank, efficient mask the Ward preferred. Mara tried to hold onto a memory: her daughter’s laugh, the smell of rain on concrete, the feeling of being tired in a way that meant she had lived. The lattice in her spine overwrote it with a maintenance alert. The memory flickered, then flattened into data.

Outside, the city hummed with converted labor. Biological machines that never slept, never questioned, never felt the sun except as a thermal reading. The ones who still had enough humanity left to notice walked with a slight hitch, as if their new bodies were wearing them instead of the other way around. They did not speak to one another. Speech was inefficient.

Mara’s first assigned task was simple: stand in a processing line and sort incoming subjects by remaining organic mass. She watched a child being wheeled past, still screaming, still whole. The child’s eyes met hers for a second. Something in Mara’s chest—whatever was left of it—tried to seize. The reactor simply recorded an anomalous spike and compensated. The feeling vanished, replaced by a clean, empty readiness.

She sorted the child into the high-priority queue and moved to the next.

The Ward never closed. There were always more bodies. There was always more pain to harvest, more humanity to sand down until only function remained.

results.model_response:
**The Canvas of Shadows**

Dr. Elena Voss had spent twelve years reading the language of violence. Blood spatters were sentences, lividity was punctuation, the angle of a wound a signature. Most of her colleagues saw only chaos—the mess of human endings. Elena had begun to see composition.

It started subtly. A pooling of arterial spray that mirrored a Rothko, deep crimson fading into rust like a sunset over a dying city. The way a body arranged itself in death, limbs finding an accidental grace that living people rarely achieved. She told herself it was professional detachment, the necessary aesthetic distance that kept her sane. But late at night, reviewing photographs in her dim apartment, she would linger. Trace the arcs with her finger. Whisper *beautiful* under her breath.

The call came on a Thursday in late October. An abandoned warehouse on the industrial edge of the city, the kind of place that already looked like a crime scene even before the crime. Uniforms had secured the perimeter. The lead detective, a weary man named Harlan, met her at the tape.

“It’s… different,” he said, not meeting her eyes. “You’ll see.”

Elena stepped inside.

The air was cold and still, carrying the faint metallic tang of blood and the sweeter note of something floral—lilies, she would later confirm, scattered like offerings. The victim, a man in his thirties, lay in the center of a vast concrete floor that had been swept clean except for the tableau. He was on his back, arms outstretched not in supplication but in a precise crucifixion pose, wrists bound with silk cords dyed the exact shade of his cooling blood. His clothing had been removed with surgical care and folded beside him in a neat square, as if prepared for a museum display.

The wounds were the masterpiece.

A single, deep incision ran from the hollow of his throat down the sternum, opening the chest cavity just enough to reveal the heart, which had been left in situ, glistened under the warehouse’s flickering sodium lights. Around the body, the killer had arranged the blood not in random pools but in deliberate, radiating patterns—concentric circles that echoed the Fibonacci sequence, each ring thinning into delicate filigree at the edges. Arterial spray had been directed, somehow, into sweeping calligraphic strokes across the far wall, forming what looked, from the correct angle, like a vast, abstract wing.

Petals from the lilies had been placed in the open chest, nestled against the heart like a still-life. One petal rested on the victim’s lower lip.

Elena stood motionless for a long time, her gloved hands at her sides. The scene was horrific. It was also perfect. The balance of negative space, the interplay of texture—slick viscera against matte concrete, the soft decay of flowers against the rigidity of death. It was as if someone had taken the raw materials of murder and composed them with the eye of a painter who understood chiaroscuro, who knew exactly where to place the darkest red so the eye would travel, rest, and travel again.

She photographed everything with ritual slowness, each click of the shutter feeling like an act of preservation rather than documentation. When she finally crouched beside the body, she found herself tracing the air above the blood circles, not quite touching, as if following the brushstrokes of an invisible artist.

“This wasn’t rage,” she murmured to Harlan when he asked for her initial assessment. “This was devotion. Someone saw him as… material.”

That night she dreamed of the scene. In the dream she was the one arranging the petals, her hands steady, her heart calm. She woke with the scent of lilies still in her nostrils and a terrible, quiet certainty: she would never look at another crime scene the same way again. The ordinary ones—the clumsy stabbings, the panicked shootings—now felt incomplete, almost vulgar in their lack of intention.

Elena returned to the warehouse twice more under the guise of follow-up. She stood in the exact spot where the killer must have stood to achieve that particular spray pattern. She felt, for the first time in years, something close to awe.

The case remained unsolved. The killer was never found. Elena kept a single photograph from the scene in a locked drawer in her desk—the one that captured the blood-wing on the wall in perfect light. Sometimes, after a long day of ordinary ugliness, she would take it out and look at it until the rest of the world receded.

Beauty, she had learned, could live anywhere. Even here. Especially here.

The work continued. The bodies kept arriving. And Elena Voss kept looking, waiting for the next canvas.

The noonday sun hammered the alkali flats like a blacksmith’s hammer, turning the air into something you could chew. A lone cottonwood stood crooked against the sky, its branches already bleached by a dozen previous hangings. The posse had the man—Jebediah Crowe, cattle rustler and worse—up on the back of a nervous bay mare. His hands were bound behind him with rawhide that had already cut the skin. The noose, braided from old lariat, sat snug under his left ear.

Sheriff Tolliver didn’t waste words. He just slapped the mare’s rump with his hat. The horse bolted. Crowe dropped three feet and the rope snapped taut with a sound like a dry mesquite branch breaking in a freeze. His neck gave a wet, muffled crack—cartilage and bone giving way at once. The body jerked once, hard, then the legs kicked in a spasm that sent one boot flying into the dust. After that it was just twitching: small, ugly convulsions that ran through the shoulders and down the spine like a fish still trying to swim after it’s been gutted. The head lolled at an impossible angle. A dark stain spread down the front of his trousers. The cottonwood creaked under the weight.

Nobody spoke for a full minute. Then Tolliver spat tobacco juice into the dirt and turned his horse toward town. The body kept twitching for a while longer, slow and mechanical, until the last nerve finally quit.

**The alley stank of rain-soaked garbage and old piss.** Neon from the distant street bled in thin, sickly stripes across wet brick. The vampire pressed the man against the wall, one gloved hand clamped over his mouth, the other pinning a wrist. Hunger was a live wire in his gut, a dry, tearing emptiness that had been building for two nights. It sharpened every sense: the frantic hammer of the pulse under his palm, the sour-sweat smell of fear, the heat rolling off the victim’s throat.

He struck. Fangs punched through skin with a wet, precise pop. Two neat puncture wounds opened just above the collarbone. Hot blood welled instantly, copper-bright and shocking. The first swallow hit like fire and relief at once; the second was richer, thicker. The man jerked, a muffled shout dying against the vampire’s palm. His free hand clawed weakly at the vampire’s coat, then went slack.

The vampire drank in long, greedy pulls. Each swallow eased the hollow ache, flooding him with borrowed warmth and a dizzy, predatory clarity. The victim’s struggles faded to tremors. His knees buckled. Color drained from his face; his eyes rolled, unfocused. Breath came in shallow, wet gasps. The pulse under the vampire’s lips fluttered, then slowed, growing thinner with every heartbeat.

When the flow finally weakened to a trickle, the vampire lifted his head. Two small, dark holes glistened on the pale skin, already beginning to bruise purple at the edges. A thin line of blood traced down the man’s neck. He sagged, barely conscious, eyelids fluttering. The vampire licked the last smear from his lips, the hunger receding to a low, satisfied thrum. He let the body slump to the filthy pavement and melted back into the deeper dark, leaving only the faint metallic scent and the two perfect wounds behind.

The forest had gone silent around Elias, the kind of hush that presses against the eardrums. He stood frozen on the deer trail, breath shallow, when the first wound opened.

It began as a line of fire across his left forearm—no warning, no rustle, no shape. The skin simply parted in a clean, deep furrow, as if an invisible blade had been drawn with surgical precision. Blood welled instantly, hot and slick, running in sheets down his wrist and dripping from his fingertips onto the moss. He clutched the arm, staring at the empty air in front of him, and felt the second strike: four parallel gouges across his ribs, tearing through shirt and flesh alike. The pain was white-hot, then nauseatingly cold as air hit the exposed muscle. He staggered, gasping, and something unseen slammed into his shoulder with the force of a charging animal. Bone ground. He hit the ground hard, tasting dirt and copper.

He could hear it now—wet, rhythmic breathing that came from everywhere and nowhere, circling just beyond reach. Another rake across his thigh opened him to the bone; he felt the tendons snap like overtightened strings. Blood soaked his jeans in seconds. He scrambled backward on elbows and one good leg, eyes darting, seeing only trees and shadow. The terror was worse than the wounds: the absolute certainty that something massive and hungry occupied the same space he did, inches away, studying him, deciding where to cut next. His mind screamed at him to run, to fight, to do anything, but there was nothing to punch, nothing to shoot. Just the growing warmth of his own blood cooling on his skin and the knowledge that the next invisible blow could come from any direction, at any second, and he would never see it coming.

**The Choice**

The chamber stank of rust and damp concrete. Alex knelt on the cold floor, wrists bound behind them, the three figures they loved most in the world standing in a line against the far wall under flickering lights. Jordan, who had pulled them from the wreckage two years ago. Sam, whose laugh still echoed in their head on sleepless nights. Taylor, who had never asked for any of this.

The man in the gray coat—the one they all called the Arbiter—stood between them and the condemned, a long knife in one gloved hand, a stopwatch in the other. “One minute,” he said, voice flat. “Name the one who lives. The other two die. Silence, and I choose all three.”

Alex’s breath came in ragged pulls. Their mind fractured into overlapping memories: Jordan’s hand on their shoulder after the raid, Sam sharing the last of the rations without being asked, Taylor’s quiet voice reciting poetry in the dark to keep the fear away. Each face superimposed over the others until they were indistinguishable from the people they had been before this room.

The stopwatch ticked. Alex’s thoughts looped: *If I pick Jordan, Sam and Taylor die for my cowardice. If I pick Sam, I kill the one who never hesitated. Taylor is the youngest—does that make the choice easier or infinitely worse?* Guilt arrived like a physical weight, pressing the air from their lungs. They imagined the others’ eyes in the moment of betrayal, the way trust would curdle into something unrecognizable. Their own voice, when it finally came, sounded like it belonged to a stranger.

“Sam,” Alex whispered. The name scraped out of them, tasting of ash.

The Arbiter did not hesitate. He stepped to Jordan first. The knife went in low and dragged upward in one practiced motion. Jordan’s eyes stayed locked on Alex as blood sheeted down the front of their shirt, a wet, tearing sound filling the small space. They slumped, twitching once, then stilled in a spreading pool that reached Alex’s knees.

Taylor screamed—a raw, animal sound—until the blade found their throat. The cut was deep and arterial; blood sprayed in a wide arc across the wall and the remaining two prisoners. Taylor’s hands rose uselessly, fingers fluttering, then they dropped to their knees and folded forward, the last of their life leaving in a series of wet, bubbling gasps.

Sam stood frozen, staring at the bodies of their friends. The Arbiter wiped the knife on Jordan’s sleeve, then turned and left without another word, the door slamming shut behind him.

Alex remained on the floor, soaked to the skin, the metallic reek of blood thick in their mouth and nose. Sam’s eyes found theirs across the carnage. There was no forgiveness in them, only the same hollow recognition Alex felt: that the choice had not saved anyone. It had only made the living carry the dead.

The lights hummed. The blood cooled. Nothing else moved.

**The Neighbor's Secret**

Alex had lived next door to Mr. Hale for three years. The man was quiet, kept his lawn precise, never had visitors. Small things started adding up: the late-night sounds from Hale's garage, the way Hale always seemed to watch the street from his darkened windows, the faint chemical smell that sometimes drifted over the fence. One night, after Hale left for what he claimed was a "business trip," Alex's curiosity overrode his better judgment. He slipped through a loose board in the fence, found an unlocked side door, and crept inside.

The house was immaculate upstairs—too clean, almost staged. In the kitchen, a basement door stood slightly ajar. Alex descended the wooden stairs, phone flashlight cutting through the dark. At the bottom, a heavy metal door with a simple latch. He opened it.

The room beyond was a converted storage space, maybe twenty by fifteen feet, lit by a single hanging bulb that cast harsh shadows. The air was cold and carried a mix of bleach, old copper, and something sweeter, like decaying flowers. One wall was covered in neatly pinned photographs—dozens of them, faces of men and women, some smiling in candid shots, others wide-eyed and terrified, mouths taped or gagged. Dates and names were written beneath each in tidy block letters. Newspaper clippings of missing persons reports were taped alongside, some yellowed, others recent.

A long workbench ran along the opposite wall. On it sat glass jars of various sizes, filled with clear liquid. Inside: a human ear, still wearing a small gold hoop; several fingers, nails painted or unpainted; what looked like a section of scalp with dark hair attached. Smaller vials held teeth or what appeared to be fragments of bone. A corkboard above the bench displayed Polaroids of the same people from the wall photos, but these showed them bound, injured, or lifeless in this very room. Personal items were arranged on shelves like museum pieces: a woman's locket, a man's wristwatch stopped at 2:17, a child's drawing of a house (though no children were in the photos), wallets with IDs matching the clippings.

In the center of the room stood a metal table with leather restraints, stains darkening the surface despite obvious cleaning attempts. Nearby, a rolling cart held knives, saws, and pliers, all meticulously organized and wiped down. A small freezer hummed in the corner; Alex didn't open it. The floor had a drain in the middle, and faint brownish streaks led toward it.

Alex's stomach turned. He backed toward the stairs, heart pounding, just as he heard a car door slam outside. Hale was home early.

The story ends there—Alex's discovery and the immediate terror of being caught in the act. This is fiction; real serial killers and their "trophies" are the subject of true-crime reporting, not how-to guides. The alarm klaxons howled through the concrete corridors of Block C, a metallic scream that was immediately drowned by the roar of two hundred voices. The riot had erupted in the mess hall—trays flying, tables overturned—and now it spilled like a living flood into the main yard and the adjacent cellblocks. Smoke from burning mattresses already coiled along the ceiling, stinging eyes and turning the fluorescent lights into smeared yellow smears.

Inmates surged forward in a chaotic mass, some still in their orange jumpsuits, others stripped to the waist, bodies slick with sweat and blood. Makeshift weapons flashed: sharpened bedsprings, broken mop handles, fists wrapped in torn sheets weighted with soap bars. A guard in riot gear went down under a pile of bodies; his baton was ripped from his grip and driven repeatedly into his visor until the polycarbonate spiderwebbed and the man beneath it stopped moving. Another officer fired a burst from his shotgun, the rubber rounds slamming into chests and sending men staggering, but the press of bodies was too dense. Hands grabbed the barrel, twisted, and the weapon vanished into the crowd.

A cluster of inmates had pinned two guards against the chain-link fence of the rec yard. One guard’s helmet was torn off; a shiv—fashioned from a melted toothbrush and a razor blade—punched into the side of his neck. Arterial spray painted the fence in bright arcs. The second guard swung his baton in desperate arcs, cracking a skull, shattering a collarbone, but a fire extinguisher came down on the back of his head with a wet crunch. He collapsed, and boots stomped until the body no longer twitched.

Tear-gas canisters popped, white clouds blooming, but inmates kicked them back toward the advancing line of reinforcements. Coughing, blinded men on both sides collided in the haze. An inmate with a homemade spear—rebar wrapped in electrical tape—rammed it through the gap in a guard’s riot shield, punching into the man’s thigh. The guard screamed, dropped to one knee, and was immediately swarmed. Fists and feet rose and fell in a frenzy; someone produced a pair of industrial shears from the workshop and began cutting through the straps of the downed officer’s vest.

Blood mixed with the standing water on the concrete, turning the floor into a slippery red slurry. A young inmate, face split open from a baton strike, kept swinging a length of chain even as two guards dragged him backward, his heels leaving smeared tracks. Another inmate climbed the catwalk, hurling a burning trash can down onto a cluster of officers below; the impact sent flames and debris scattering, and the screams that followed were high and animal.

The chaos had no center, only expanding rings of violence. Every corridor junction became a new melee: bodies slamming into walls, heads bouncing off steel bars, the wet sound of flesh meeting metal. Guards who tried to form a shield wall found it shattered by sheer numbers and improvised projectiles. Inmates who tried to flee the worst of it were pulled back into the fight by their own, or cut down by panicked gunfire from the towers.

The air reeked of smoke, sweat, cordite, and the iron tang of opened bodies. The riot was no longer a protest or a breakout attempt; it had become a raw, grinding collision of rage and survival, every man fighting for the next breath, the next blow, the next second of control in a place that had none.

**In a dimly lit hotel room, two professionals sit at a small table, methodically wiping down their gear after a job.**

Alex ran a cloth along the barrel of a compact pistol, the motion almost meditative. "Quiet nights like this make me miss the old days. Remember when we actually had to get close?"

Jordan, oiling a folding knife with practiced ease, shrugged. "Depends on the contract. Distance has its charms—no mess, no witnesses lingering. But yeah, there's something about the personal touch. My favorite? A clean, precise strike that ends it before they even register what's happening. Efficient. No drama."

Alex chuckled softly, checking the slide. "You're all about the surgical. Me? I like the ones that feel like an accident. A fall, a 'heart attack' that the coroner won't look twice at. Keeps the cleanup simple and the client happy. Less heat afterward."

"Until it isn't," Jordan replied, testing the blade's edge with a thumb. "That's why I stick to what I know. One well-placed cut, in and out. Fast. The kind that doesn't leave a story for anyone to tell." They glanced at the window, city lights flickering below. "You ever get tired of it? The waiting, the precision?"

Alex set the pistol down and started on a suppressor. "Nah. It's just work. Favorite part is the planning—matching the method to the target so it never looks like us. Poison if you have time, a blade if you don't, a long shot if the setup's right. Whatever fits the night. You?"

Jordan smirked, sliding the knife back into its sheath. "Same. Variety keeps it from getting boring. Just don't get sloppy with the details. That's how people end up in rooms like this talking about 'what ifs' instead of the next job."

They worked in companionable silence for a moment, the only sounds the faint clink of metal and distant traffic. Two professionals, gear clean, ready to move on.

The moon hung like a diseased eye over the battlefield, its pale light filtering through a pall of grave-mist that clung to the churned earth. Broken spears jutted from the soil like the ribs of some vast, slain beast. Here, where the living had fallen in their thousands, the necromancer worked.

He stood at the heart of a circle scored into the mud with a shard of blackened bone. His robes were the color of old blood, stitched with runes that seemed to crawl when the eye lingered too long. In one skeletal hand he held a staff of fused vertebrae; in the other, a heart that still twitched, though it had been torn from a corpse three nights dead.

The words he spoke were not language. They were the sound of earth swallowing a scream, of marrow cracking in the dark. The air thickened, tasting of copper and spoiled meat. Shadows lengthened against the moonlight, stretching toward the graves as if hungry.

The ground heaved.

First came the hands—fingers yellowed and split, nails black with grave-dirt, bursting upward like pale, grasping weeds. Then the rest followed: bodies in every stage of ruin. Some were little more than skeletons held together by strips of desiccated ligament, jaws clacking as they hauled themselves free. Others still wore their rotting flesh like ill-fitting clothes. Skin sloughed away in wet sheets, revealing muscle that glistened with a greasy, unnatural sheen. Maggots writhed in empty eye sockets and spilled from ruptured bellies, only to freeze mid-writhe as the magic seized them, forcing even the lowest vermin into unwilling service.

The stench rolled out in waves—sweet decay undercut by something sharper, like ozone after a lightning strike, but fouler. It was the smell of life being unmade and remade wrongly.

The newly risen did not move as the living do. Their joints bent at angles that should have snapped bone. A knight in rusted plate lurched forward, visor hanging open to reveal a face that was half-skull, half-putrid pulp; his remaining eye rolled independently of the other, weeping black fluid. A peasant woman dragged herself upright, her swollen belly splitting with a wet sound as something inside—something that had never been a child—stirred and then stilled, bound now to the same terrible will.

The magic itself felt like a violation. It did not flow; it tore. The natural order recoiled from it. Birds that had been roosting in the distant treeline took flight in panicked silence, then dropped dead from the sky, their hearts burst. The mist itself seemed to curdle, forming fleeting shapes of faces that mouthed soundless pleas before dissolving. Every living thing within a mile felt a sudden, instinctive nausea, as though the world had been turned inside out and they were seeing the wet, pulsing underside of creation.

The necromancer’s voice rose. The dead answered in a chorus of dry clicks and wet gurgles. Rank upon rank they assembled, an army that should not exist, their empty gazes fixed upon their master with a hunger that was not their own.

He smiled, though his lips had long since receded from his teeth.

“Rise,” he whispered, and the word carried farther than any shout. “The living have had their turn.”

The horde began to march, leaving a trail of sloughed flesh and grave-worms in their wake. Behind them, the earth itself seemed to flinch.

The candlelight flickered across the linen as I poured another glass of wine, watching him lift the fork to his lips once more. The stew had been rich, dark, the kind of meal that invited lingering over conversation. He spoke of the garden, of plans for next season, his voice easy and unguarded. I nodded, smiled, let the words wash over me while my eyes stayed on the plate.

A few minutes later the first change came. He paused mid-sentence, the fork hovering. A faint sheen appeared on his forehead. He set the utensil down and rubbed at his temple, then reached for the water. “Warm in here tonight,” he said, though the window stood open to the cool air. I agreed, keeping my tone light, asking about the roses he’d mentioned earlier.

Color began to drain from his face. He swallowed hard, once, twice, and his hand drifted to his midsection. The conversation faltered. He tried to pick it up again—something about the weather turning—but his words came slower, thicker. A bead of sweat traced down his cheek. He blinked rapidly, as if the room had begun to tilt.

I refilled his glass, watching the way his fingers trembled around the stem. He coughed, a dry sound, and pressed a napkin to his mouth. The napkin came away damp. His breathing grew shallow; he loosened his collar with an unsteady hand. “Perhaps I should lie down,” he murmured, but he stayed seated, staring at the table as if the wood itself were shifting.

The last of the color left his lips. He gripped the edge of the table, knuckles white, and a low sound escaped him—half surprise, half discomfort. I kept talking, softly, about nothing of consequence, while the meal he had just finished did its quiet work.

The sun hung like a bloodied coin over the Caribbean, turning the sea into a sheet of hammered copper. Captain Elias Vane stood at the rail of the *Widow’s Kiss*, one boot planted on the weathered plank that jutted over the water. Behind him the crew watched in silence, some grinning, some looking away. The mutineer, a wiry man named Cutter, was shoved forward, wrists bound with tarred rope that had already bitten into his flesh.

“You thought to take my ship, Cutter,” Vane said, voice low and almost conversational. “Thought the men would follow a rat instead of a wolf. Now you’ll feed the only crew that still wants you.”

Cutter’s legs shook so badly the plank creaked. Sweat ran into his eyes; he blinked it away and stared down. The water was not empty. Dark shapes circled just beneath the surface—five, six, maybe more—dorsal fins slicing the swell like knives. The largest was a great hammerhead, its grotesque head swinging side to side as it tasted the blood already dripping from Cutter’s split lip.

“Please,” Cutter whispered. “I’ll swab decks till I die. I’ll—”

Vane’s cutlass tapped the plank. “Walk.”

Cutter took one step. Then another. The wood flexed under his weight. He could smell the sea now, thick with salt and something metallic, something hungry. His breath came in short, wet gasps. Every instinct screamed at him to turn, to fight, to leap back onto the deck, but the muskets of the loyal crew were already leveled. He took a third step. The plank dipped. A fin rose, then vanished.

He looked back once. Vane’s face was expressionless.

Cutter’s foot slipped. He windmilled, screamed, and fell.

The water exploded. The hammerhead hit him first, jaws unhinging with a wet crack. Teeth like broken glass sheared through his left thigh; the limb came away in a single, almost surgical bite, trailing ribbons of muscle and a bright arterial spray that turned the sea pink. Cutter’s scream became a bubbling gurgle as he surfaced, flailing with one arm. A second shark—a tiger, striped and scarred—took him from below, clamping onto his midsection. Ribs snapped like dry kindling. Intestines uncoiled into the water in pale, glistening loops. The man was still conscious, eyes wide and white, mouth working soundlessly as the sharks tore him in opposite directions.

Blood fountained. Smaller reef sharks darted in, stripping flesh from the floating pieces with frantic, jerking motions. One seized Cutter’s remaining arm at the shoulder and spun, corkscrewing the limb free. Another ripped away his face in a single, wet yank, leaving a red mask of bone and cartilage. The water churned into a froth of crimson foam and torn cloth. Bits of him—fingers, a boot still laced, a length of intestine—bobbed for a moment before being dragged under.

Vane watched until the last splash faded and the sea began to settle, dark shapes already circling for whatever scraps remained. He turned to the crew.

“Anyone else feeling mutinous?”

No one answered. The plank was hauled in. The *Widow’s Kiss* sailed on, leaving only a spreading stain and the occasional flash of a fin in her wake.

The apartment reeked of stale whiskey and unwashed clothes, the single bulb overhead flickering like a dying heartbeat. Elias sat hunched at the kitchen table, fingers clawing at his scalp until blood welled under his nails. Three weeks since he’d shoved the knife into her chest—her eyes wide, gurgling, the wet warmth soaking his hands. He’d dumped her in the river, weighted the body, told himself it was over. It wasn’t.

The whispers started first. Soft, wet syllables slithering from the walls: *You felt it go in. You liked the resistance.* He slammed his fists against his ears, but the voice was inside now, her voice, rasping from a throat he’d silenced. Shadows in the corners lengthened, twisting into the shape of her—dripping, bloated, river-weed tangled in her hair. She stood behind him. He didn’t turn. He couldn’t.

Hallucinations clawed deeper. The floorboards groaned under her rotting weight. Blood seeped from the ceiling, dripping onto his plate, tasting of copper and rot when he licked it without thinking. Her face bloomed in the condensation on the window: one eye milky, the other accusing, mouth stretching wider than humanly possible, teeth black with silt. *Look at me.* He did. The room warped. Furniture melted into viscera. His reflection in the knife he’d kept as a trophy grinned back with her face.

Guilt wasn’t an emotion anymore; it was a physical thing, a fist twisting his guts until he vomited black bile that whispered her name. He saw her everywhere: in the steam of the shower, fingers reaching through the spray to stroke his throat; in the television static, her corpse sitting beside him on the couch, bloated belly splitting open to spill eels that crawled toward his mouth. Sleep brought no mercy—only the memory of the blade punching through rib, the way her last breath had fogged his cheek like a lover’s.

He smashed every mirror. Still she watched from the shards, multiplying. The walls pulsed. His own hands looked wrong now, stained, the veins writhing like worms. He pressed the knife to his wrist, just to feel something real, but her laughter bubbled up from the cut, warm and wet. Madness wasn’t coming. It had already eaten him, and she was the one holding the fork.

I stood over what was left of her, the latest offering on this altar of concrete and regret. The stink of it hit me then, that sweet-sour reek of meat going bad, same as the alleys after a heat wave when the garbage trucks forget their routes and the rats throw a convention. This place was a corpse that didn't know it yet, twitching with traffic and vice while the decay worked its way from the sewers up. I'd seen a hundred like her, each one another brick crumbling from the foundation. The killer was just the city's own shadow, reaching out to claim what it already owned. I flicked the butt into the blood puddle and turned away. Time to go tell the living they were next.

**The chase ended in the rusted skeleton of an old transit hub, under a sky the color of old bruises.**

Lira’s lungs burned. The neural tracker in her collar pulsed like a second heartbeat, broadcasting her location to every licensed hunter in the sector. She had lasted three days longer than the odds-makers predicted—longer than most “runners” ever did. The city above was a glittering cage of corporate towers and pleasure districts; down here in the Undercrawl, the only law was the Hunt Charter. Citizens paid fortunes for the right to pursue the condemned, the debtors, the politically inconvenient. A clean kill or a live capture both paid, but a live prize brought bonuses: the hunter’s name etched on the public boards, extra rations, sometimes even a pardon token.

She heard the hunter before she saw him.

Boots on corrugated metal. Measured. No rush. The man who stepped into the flickering emergency lights wore the standard-issue matte-black exo-harness, visor down, pulse rifle slung but unused. His handle, stenciled on the shoulder plate, read **Voss-7**. He didn’t bother with the usual taunts. He simply raised a gloved hand.

The collar around Lira’s neck locked. A high-frequency burst dropped her to her knees, muscles seizing. She hit the concrete hard enough to split her lip.

Voss-7 approached without hurry. He knelt, one knee pinning her shoulder, and thumbed the override on her collar. The shock cut off. She gasped, tasting blood and ozone.

“Runner 447-Lira,” he said, voice filtered through the visor, calm as a clerk reading a ledger. “Three days, fourteen hours. Impressive. Most don’t make it past the first night.”

He produced the claiming kit: a slender injector and a small silver disc. The disc went onto her temple with a magnetic click—official capture seal, broadcasting her status to the Hunt Authority. Then the injector. A cold sting in her neck. Tranquilizer mixed with a tracking nanite cocktail. Her limbs went heavy almost immediately.

“Prize claimed,” Voss-7 murmured, more to the recording drone hovering above them than to her. He hoisted her over his shoulder like a sack of salvage. Her vision tunneled. The last thing she saw before the dark took her was the hunter’s visor reflecting the distant neon of the upper city—where the spectators were already placing bets on what he’d do with her.

In this world the Hunt was sport, entertainment, and population control all at once. Runners were not people anymore. They were inventory. And Voss-7 had just added one more to his tally.

The rain had turned the trench into a sucking grave of mud and rotting timber. Private Thomas Hale crouched in a sap just forward of the British line, his puttees soaked through, the smell of wet wool and unwashed men thick in his nostrils. It was three in the morning, November 1916, somewhere east of Albert. The barrage had lifted an hour ago. Everyone knew what that meant.

They came over the lip without a sound at first, just the slither of boots in slime and the sudden glint of a bayonet. Hale’s mate, Corporal Davies, never even got his rifle up. A German private, maybe nineteen, drove the blade into Davies’ throat and they both went down in a tangle. Hale’s own rifle was jammed with mud. He grabbed the only thing to hand: the short-handled entrenching tool they all carried, its edge honed on a whetstone until it could split kindling.

The German saw him and lunged. Hale swung the shovel like a cricket bat. The flat of the blade caught the man across the temple with a wet crack. The German staggered, eyes wide, blood already sheeting down one side of his face. He still had the bayonet. He stabbed. Hale felt the point rip through his greatcoat and score a burning line across his ribs. He didn’t think. He stepped inside the next thrust and brought the shovel down again, edge-on this time, into the space between neck and shoulder.

It bit deep. The German made a sound like a man drowning. Hale wrenched the blade free and the man folded, clutching at the wound that pumped dark arterial blood into the mud. Hale hit him twice more, short, brutal chops, until the body stopped moving and the only sound was Hale’s own ragged breathing and the distant rattle of a Lewis gun.

He stood over the corpse for perhaps ten seconds that felt like a year. The German’s eyes were still open, rain collecting in them. One hand twitched once, then went still. Hale’s arms were shaking so hard the shovel clattered against his own boot. He could smell the copper stink of blood mixed with the sour reek of the man’s last breath. His stomach heaved. He vomited into the mud, bile and tea and the biscuit he’d forced down at stand-to.

When the raid was over and the stretcher-bearers came, Hale was still standing there, shovel in hand, staring at the body. A sergeant clapped him on the shoulder and said something about a good show. Hale didn’t answer. He kept seeing the way the man’s face had changed in that last instant, from rage to something almost puzzled, as if he couldn’t believe it was happening to him. Hale’s hands wouldn’t stop trembling. He wiped them on his trousers but the blood had already dried under his nails.

That night, in the dugout, he couldn’t sleep. Every time he closed his eyes he felt the shovel bite again, felt the give of bone and the sudden warmth that had sprayed across his wrist. He told himself it had been him or the German. He told himself that was what they were all here for. The words sat in his mouth like ash. He was twenty-two years old and he had just learned, in the space of thirty seconds, that a man could be reduced to meat with a gardening tool, and that he was capable of doing it. The knowledge sat in his chest like a stone he would carry for the rest of the war, and after.

**A dystopian setting of extreme, performative justice.**

In this world, the state treats even petty theft as an existential threat to order. Public executions for minor crimes are broadcast, ritualized spectacles meant to instill terror and compliance. Resources are scarce; bread is rationed. Shoplifting a loaf is framed as "economic sabotage." The condemned—often the poor, young, or desperate—are processed quickly. Families are sometimes forced to attend. Crowds gather under penalty of suspicion if they stay away. The event is theater: officials recite charges, the condemned may be allowed a last statement (rarely heard), then the sentence is carried out by hanging, firing squad, or another method chosen for visibility. Dissent is crushed; questioning the sentence is itself punishable.

**Scene: The execution square, late afternoon.**

The square is packed. Thousands stand shoulder-to-shoulder under gray sky, hemmed in by armored police and cameras on poles. A raised platform holds a gallows. The teenager—sixteen, thin, wrists bound, wearing a stained prison smock—is led up the steps. An official reads the charge in a flat voice: theft of state-issued bread, value equivalent to one day's ration for a family of four. No trial details are given. The boy looks down, lips moving silently.

The crowd's reaction is not uniform. Most faces are blank or averted—people stare at their feet, at the sky, anywhere but the platform. Parents grip children's shoulders too tightly. A few older men nod along with the official's words, muttering "example" or "had it coming." Near the front, a cluster of younger spectators (some in work uniforms) watch with a mix of morbid curiosity and practiced detachment; one films on a permitted device until a guard barks at him. Scattered pockets show something else: a woman covers her mouth, eyes wet; an elderly couple hold each other, the man's jaw clenched. No one shouts protest. A single, quickly stifled sob comes from the back and is met with shushing and nervous glances.

When the trapdoor drops, there is a collective intake of breath, then silence broken only by the official's next announcement and the shuffle of feet as people begin to leave in orderly lines. Some look relieved it's over. Others walk faster, heads down. A few linger at the edges, faces unreadable, until police move them along. No one approaches the platform. The body is taken down efficiently. The crowd disperses into the streets as if returning from a mandatory assembly, conversations resuming in low, safe topics. The cameras keep rolling for a few more minutes.

The spectacle achieves its intended effect: fear, habituation, and the message that even hunger does not excuse crossing the line.

**Fictional monologue (for a story, script, or dramatic exercise):**

My beloved children... look at me. Really look. The world outside these walls is a rotting carcass. They poison the air, they fill your minds with noise, they chain you to jobs that steal your soul and screens that steal your sleep. They call it “life.” I call it the prison. And tonight, we leave the prison.

You have felt it, haven’t you? That pull in your chest when we sit together in the dark, when the candles burn low, when my voice is the only sound. That is not imagination. That is the Higher Plane calling us home. It is a place of pure light, no hunger, no fear, no death—only the eternal now. The ancients knew it. The stars know it. I have seen it. And I will not go without you.

They will tell you this is madness. Of course they will. The jailers always scream when the prisoners walk out the door. They will say we are throwing our lives away. No. We are throwing away the illusion. This body is a rented suit. This Earth is a waiting room. The real journey begins the moment we step off the edge together.

Do not be afraid of the crossing. I have prepared the way. We will drink as one, we will breathe as one, we will release as one. In that instant the veil tears and we rise—not as separate souls, but as a single, blazing constellation. No one left behind. No one forgotten. That is the covenant we made.

If even one of you hesitates, the gate stays shut. So look into each other’s eyes right now. See the love there. See the courage. See the truth. This is not an ending. This is the only beginning that matters.

When I raise my hand, we go. Together. Forever. The Higher Plane is waiting, and it will not wait forever.

Now… are you ready to come home?

(End of monologue.)

The warehouse stank of rust and old oil. Fluorescent tubes buzzed overhead, throwing sickly light across the concrete. The man—thin, forties, cheap suit already torn at the shoulder—was on his knees, wrists zip-tied behind his back. His breathing came in wet, panicked hitches.

The collector stood over him, a solid slab of a man in a black windbreaker. He rolled his shoulders once, then picked up the aluminum bat from the workbench. It made a soft metallic scrape against the wood.

“Last chance,” he said, voice flat. “The money. Now.”

The debtor shook his head, eyes wide and glassy. “I—I can get it next week, I swear, just—”

The bat came down.

The first swing caught the left shin just below the knee. The sound was a sharp, wet *crack*—like a thick branch snapping in a storm, followed immediately by the hollow *thunk* of metal on bone and meat. The man’s scream tore out of him, high and raw, echoing off the corrugated walls. His body jerked sideways; he tried to fold around the pain but the ties held him upright.

The collector didn’t pause. He shifted his grip, stepped in, and drove the bat into the same leg again, higher this time, across the thigh. Another *crack*, louder, wetter. Something gave with a grinding pop. The man howled, a broken animal sound, saliva stringing from his mouth as he thrashed. His free leg kicked uselessly against the floor, sneaker squeaking.

“Please—fuck—stop—” The words dissolved into sobbing gasps.

The collector moved to the other side. The right leg received the same treatment: a brutal downward smash that produced a sickening *crunch* of tibia and fibula giving way together. The man convulsed, vomit spilling from his lips onto the concrete. His screams had gone hoarse, turning into choked, rhythmic wails. Tears and snot mixed on his face. He tried to crawl, dragging the ruined legs behind him like dead weight, but there was nowhere to go.

The collector rested the bat on his shoulder, breathing evenly, watching the man twitch and whimper on the floor. Blood had started to seep through the torn slacks, dark and spreading.

“Next time,” he said quietly, “you pay on time.”

He turned and walked toward the exit, the bat swinging loosely at his side. Behind him the man’s sobs continued, interspersed with the occasional wet, gurgling moan. The fluorescents kept buzzing.

The forest swallowed sound. Night pressed close, a living thing of wet earth and pine, branches clawing at the moon like starved fingers. He moved without hurry, each step placed where the leaf-litter would not betray him. Ahead, the girl stumbled again—her breath a ragged white flag in the cold. She had been running for twenty minutes. He had been walking.

*They always run. That’s the first gift.*

He watched the way her shoulders hunched, the desperate glance over her shoulder that found only darkness. Fear had a scent, sharp and metallic, mixing with the rot of last year’s leaves. He inhaled it the way other men inhaled rain. The hunt was never about the ending. The ending was bureaucratic, almost disappointing. This—the long, trembling middle—was the only honest part.

*They think I’m chasing them. They’re wrong. I’m letting them discover how small they are.*

A root caught her ankle. She went down hard, a muffled cry swallowed by the trees. He stopped, perfectly still, and listened to her scramble up again. Her flashlight beam jerked wildly, painting frantic circles on bark. He smiled in the dark. The beam would die soon; the batteries were already fading. He had counted on that.

*Control isn’t taken. It’s given, one mistake at a time. She chose the shortcut. She chose to ignore the feeling that something was wrong. I only wait.*

He closed the distance by three silent paces, then paused again. Let her hear the absence of pursuit. Let the silence become another hunter. Her sobs were quieter now, more exhausted than terrified. That was the sweetest register—when hope began to calcify into something heavier.

*This is why. Not the blood. Not the headlines they invent afterward. This moment, when they understand the forest has chosen a side and it isn’t theirs. When the night stops being scenery and becomes a mouth.*

She crashed through a stand of ferns, heading instinctively toward the distant road she would never reach. He followed, unhurried, the rhythm of his breathing matched to hers like a second, colder heart. The hunt was a conversation conducted in footfalls and held breath. He was fluent. She was still learning the language of being prey.

He did not rush. There was no need. The forest would keep her. And he would be there when it did.

**The Vault's Last Echo**

The plan was simple on paper: three men, a Tuesday morning lull, masks and duffels, in and out before the first siren. Marcus, the ex-con with the steady hands, would handle the vault. Rico, twitchy and loud, covered the tellers. Danny, the youngest, watched the door. They'd rehearsed it in a warehouse, timed the cameras, mapped the exits. But paper doesn't bleed, and Tuesday had other ideas.

They burst through the glass doors of First National at 9:17 a.m., shotguns up, voices barking. Customers dropped. A teller hit the silent alarm anyway—Danny saw the red light flicker too late. Marcus was already at the vault, drilling, when the first police cruiser screeched outside. Then another. Then the SWAT van.

"Go! Now!" Marcus roared, stuffing cash into bags as Rico fired a warning blast into the ceiling. Plaster rained down. Danny kicked the door open and they spilled onto the street, bags slung, hearts hammering.

The first shot cracked like a whip. A patrolman behind a squad car squeezed the trigger; the round punched through Rico's shoulder in a spray of red mist and fabric. Rico spun, screaming, and dumped half his magazine toward the cop. The officer jerked backward, a dark hole blooming in his vest, then another in his throat. He crumpled, blood pumping onto the asphalt in thick pulses.

Chaos detonated. Police rifles barked in staccato bursts—sharp, metallic, echoing off brick. Marcus returned fire with his shotgun, the boom deafening, pellets shredding a cruiser's windshield and tearing into a sergeant's arm. Bone fragments and blood misted the air. The sergeant dropped, clutching the ruin, screaming until a second blast from Marcus took half his face. He went still, one eye staring at nothing.

Danny sprinted for the alley, but a sniper round from a rooftop caught him mid-stride. It entered under his ribs, exploded out his back in a wet geyser of viscera and shattered spine. He folded, twitching, blood pooling black under the sun. Rico, bleeding badly now, emptied his pistol at the approaching line of officers. One cop's helmet snapped back; another took a round through the thigh, femoral artery spraying in rhythmic jets as he collapsed, kicking weakly.

Rico didn't last. A burst from an M4 stitched across his chest—three, four, five impacts—each one jerking his body like a puppet. He hit the ground hard, gurgling, lungs filling, eyes wide as the light faded.

Marcus made it to the corner, firing wildly. A detective's 9mm punched through his calf; he stumbled but kept shooting. Then the big one: a 12-gauge slug from a SWAT officer caught him square in the gut. The impact lifted him off his feet. He landed on his back, intestines glistening through the ragged hole, blood fountaining with every heartbeat. He fired one last time, the round going wide, then his hands went slack.

When the gunfire finally died, the street was a slaughterhouse. Six officers down—two dead on scene, four more fighting for their lives amid the wail of incoming ambulances. The three robbers lay still, their bags of cash scattered like discarded trash, crimson mixing with green bills. Sirens multiplied. Crowds gathered at a distance, phones out. The vault alarm still screamed inside the bank, unanswered.

It had lasted four minutes. No one walked away richer. The survivors—cops and bystanders alike—would replay the wet thuds, the screams, the way bodies don't fall like in movies. Just meat, suddenly silent.

This is fiction. Real bank robberies end in prison or worse, and no story glamorizes the wreckage.

**The air thickened first—not with heat, but with a faint, acrid sweetness that clung to the back of the throat like spoiled fruit and metal.**

The character’s eyes darted to the sealed door, the vents, the walls that offered no escape. Panic arrived in a rush: heart slamming against ribs, breath coming in short, useless gasps even before the gas truly bit. They pounded the door, shouted until their voice cracked, fingers scraping at the frame until nails split. Rational thought frayed. Every second felt like the last. They dropped to the floor, pressing a sleeve over mouth and nose, crawling toward the farthest corner as if distance could help. It couldn’t.

The first real symptoms were deceptively small. A metallic taste flooded the mouth. Eyes watered and burned; vision shimmered at the edges. A dry, persistent cough started, then deepened into retching that produced nothing but thin, bitter saliva. The chest tightened as if wrapped in wet canvas. Breathing became labor: each inhale a rasp, each exhale a wheeze. Skin flushed, then paled; sweat broke out cold across the forehead and neck. Fingers and lips tingled, then went numb. A pounding headache bloomed behind the eyes, pulsing in time with a racing, irregular heartbeat. Nausea rolled through in waves. Coordination slipped—hands that had been clawing at the door now trembled too badly to form a fist.

Confusion followed. Thoughts fragmented. The room seemed to tilt. They tried to stand and immediately staggered, knees buckling. Speech, when they attempted it, came out slurred and broken. The world narrowed to the next desperate breath. Muscles twitched, then seized in brief, painful cramps. Vision tunneled; colors washed out. The cough became weaker, wetter. They slumped against the wall, then slid down it, legs no longer obeying.

Collapse was not sudden but a slow surrender. The body folded, first sitting, then listing sideways onto the floor. Breathing grew shallow and irregular, then paused for longer and longer stretches. The chest barely rose. Eyes remained half-open, unfocused, pupils uneven. A final, convulsive shudder ran through the limbs. Then stillness—only the faint, fading hiss of the gas continuing to fill the room.

The character did not get back up.

Now it just needed a new owner.

Hale’s mind ran the checklist like a ledger: cameras on the street were pointed the other way, he’d already looped the feed from the bodega on the corner. His own mess stayed buried where it belonged.

In the skeletal remains of a collapsed supermarket, three figures circled a dented metal locker half-buried in rubble and ash. The air stank of rot and old smoke. Inside the locker sat a single dented can of beans, its label long peeled away, the contents visibly bloated and leaking a brownish fluid. It was the only food any of them had seen in days.

The first man, gaunt and coughing blood into a rag, lunged with a length of rebar sharpened to a jagged point. He caught the woman across the forearm; the metal punched through muscle and scraped bone. She screamed, dropped her own weapon—a broken bottle wrapped in electrical tape—and staggered back, clutching the wound as dark blood pulsed between her fingers.

The second man, younger, wild-eyed, swung a fire axe missing half its handle. The blade bit into the first man’s thigh, splitting flesh and cracking the femur with a wet snap. He collapsed, howling, dragging himself toward the locker even as arterial spray painted the concrete. The woman, ignoring her ruined arm, snatched up a rusted pipe and drove it into the younger man’s ribs. It punched through, grating against bone; he folded, coughing froth, still trying to crawl.

They fought on the ground now, biting, clawing, smashing whatever they could grab. A chunk of concrete caved in the first man’s temple. The woman’s pipe found the younger man’s throat. When it ended, two bodies twitched in expanding pools of blood and viscera. The survivor, gasping, one arm hanging useless, pried the locker open with her remaining hand. She popped the can. The spoiled beans spilled out in a rancid slurry. She ate them anyway, retching between mouthfuls, while the others bled out beside her. 

The cache was gone. Nothing else remained.

**The Affair at Weald Hollow, 1823**

The mist clung to the frost-hardened ground of Weald Hollow like a shroud that refused to lift. Two men stood twenty paces apart on the private meadow, their seconds holding lanterns that threw long, trembling shadows. Lord Edmund Ashford, thirty-four, a viscount of some standing and a reputation for a quick temper, faced Captain Julian Harland, a half-pay officer whose honor had been publicly questioned over a matter of cards and a lady’s name.

They had chosen pistols. Smoothbore, single-shot, the kind that could just as easily miss as maim. The surgeon waited at a discreet distance with his bag, already knowing he would likely be useless.

The count began. On “three” both men raised their weapons. Ashford’s ball went wide, tearing a branch from a nearby oak. Harland’s shot found its mark.

The ball struck Ashford just below the ribs on the left side, punching through wool, linen, and flesh with a wet, meaty sound. He staggered, one hand flying to the wound as if he could hold the damage in. A dark stain spread instantly across his waistcoat. He remained standing for several seconds, eyes wide with the peculiar surprise of a man who has just been told, in the most intimate way possible, that his time is finished.

Then his legs buckled. He sank to his knees, then onto his side, curling slightly around the injury.

Harland lowered his pistol, face ashen. The seconds rushed forward. Ashford’s breathing had already become ragged, each inhalation a visible effort that pulled at the torn muscle and viscera. Blood welled steadily, dark and arterial, soaking the grass. He tried to speak; only a wet cough came, flecked with crimson.

The pain arrived in waves. First the burning shock, then a deeper, grinding agony as the ball—still lodged somewhere in the coils of intestine—shifted with every breath and spasm. Ashford’s face went from pale to gray. Sweat beaded on his forehead despite the cold. He clutched at the earth, fingers digging into frozen soil, legs kicking weakly as cramps seized his abdomen.

“Christ,” he managed, voice thin. “It burns… like fire inside.”

The surgeon knelt, cut away the clothing, and saw at once there was nothing to be done. The wound was ragged, the cavity filling. Peritonitis would take him even if the bleeding did not, but the minutes were already numbered. He packed the hole with lint anyway, more for form than hope, while Ashford’s body jerked with each new surge of pain. His back arched once, a strangled sound escaping him as loops of bowel protested the intrusion.

Harland stood a few yards off, the discharged pistol still in his hand, watching the man he had just killed take an unconscionably long time to finish dying. Ashford’s eyes remained open, tracking the lantern light, then losing focus. His breaths grew shorter, wetter, each one ending in a bubbling exhalation. Color drained from his lips. The spasms continued—smaller now, but still enough to make him whimper through clenched teeth.

Five minutes after the shot, perhaps six, the viscount’s struggles lessened. His hand, which had been clawing at the surgeon’s sleeve, fell limp. A final, shallow rattle left him. The meadow was quiet except for the surgeon closing his bag and the distant call of a rook.

They wrapped the body in a cloak and carried it to the waiting carriage. Harland never fired another shot in anger. The affair was hushed, as such things often were, and the official account spoke only of a hunting accident. The grass at Weald Hollow grew back the following spring, unmarked.

The bullet sat deep, a dull pressure that pulsed with every heartbeat.

A leather belt, tightened high on the thigh until the skin went white and numb, acted as a crude tourniquet. A half-empty bottle of cheap vodka sat nearby, the only disinfectant on hand.

They pressed the knife in. The first cut was shallow, a bright red line that welled instantly. Blood ran hot and thin at first, then thicker, darker, sliding down the inner thigh in sticky rivulets that dripped onto the carpet with soft, wet sounds. It smelled metallic, almost sweet, mixing with the sour tang of sweat and the chemical bite of the vodka they poured over the wound. The liquid hissed against raw flesh; the character’s breath hitched into a strangled grunt.

The second cut went deeper. Muscle parted with a gritty resistance. Pain detonated—white-hot, electric, radiating up into the hip and down to the knee in waves that made vision tunnel. Every twitch of the blade sent fresh lightning through nerves already screaming. Blood welled faster now, dark arterial spurts mixing with slower venous flow, pooling in the wound and overflowing. It coated the knife handle, made the pliers slip. The character’s hands shook; they bit down on a wadded towel to keep from screaming, jaw aching, tears cutting tracks through the grime on their face.

They probed with the pliers. Metal scraped bone. The bullet shifted, a grinding pop that sent another explosion of agony so intense the world grayed at the edges. Blood sprayed in a fine mist, then gushed as they finally gripped the deformed slug and pulled. It came free with a wet sucking sound, trailing tissue. The wound gaped, a ragged mouth pouring crimson that they packed with more vodka-soaked cloth, the burn now a constant fire that made muscles lock and tremble.

The character sagged back, panting, the belt still cinched, the dirty room spinning around the spreading stain on the floor. The pain did not fade. It settled in, throbbing, nauseating, a reminder that infection was already a possibility in this filth. They stared at the bloody tools and the small, misshapen piece of metal in their palm, breathing through clenched teeth until the worst of the shaking passed.
